summary: The Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes are three peoples who share one reservation in northwestern Montana: the Séliš (Salish), the Qlispé (Pend d'Oreille), and the Ksanka band of the Kootenai. The Salish and Pend d'Oreille speak closely related dialects of the Salish language family, while the Kootenai language is not known to be related to any other. Their homelands once reached across western Montana and into Idaho, British Columbia, and Wyoming. The 1855 Hellgate Treaty set aside the Flathead Reservation, though tribal leaders understood its boundaries to be larger than the written text. Chief Charlo and the Salish refused for decades to give up their Bitterroot Valley homeland. In October 1891, under Army escort, they made the move north that some historians call Montana's Trail of Tears. In 1910 the government opened reservation land to homesteaders, and much of the best farmland, including most of the Mission Valley, passed out of tribal hands. The tribes have been buying land back ever since and again own most of the reservation. In 2015 they took ownership of the hydroelectric dam on the lower Flathead River, now called the Séliš Ksanka Qlispé Dam. The tribal government is based in Pablo, also home to Salish Kootenai College and the People's Center museum.

summary: Two nations share the Fort Belknap Reservation in north-central Montana: the Aaniiih, the White Clay People, long called Gros Ventre in English, and the Nakoda, or Assiniboine. Aaniiih history tells of a long-ago parting from the people who became the Arapaho, and the two are still counted as relatives. The Nakoda at Fort Belknap are kin to Nakoda families at Fort Peck and in Canada. Smallpox struck the Aaniiih again and again in the 1700s and 1800s, and the end of the buffalo brought hunger to the Milk River country. In 1888 a vast reserve the two nations had shared with the Blackfeet and others across northern Montana was broken into three smaller reservations: Fort Belknap, Fort Peck, and Blackfeet. In the 1890s, after miners found gold in the Little Rocky Mountains, the government took a strip of those mountains from the reservation. Tribal members understood the deal differently, and it remains in dispute. The two nations once handled their affairs separately. Under the Indian Reorganization Act they adopted a shared constitution as the Fort Belknap Indian Community, with council seats for both. The government is based at Fort Belknap Agency, and Aaniiih Nakoda College, on the reservation, teaches the White Clay and Nakoda languages.

summary: The Fort Peck Reservation in northeastern Montana is home to two nations: the Nakoda, or Assiniboine, and the Sioux, made up of Dakota and Lakota bands. The three peoples speak related languages, and their histories reach back to the country between the Mississippi River and Lake Superior. Over generations the Nakoda moved north into Cree country and onto the northern Plains, where they became longtime allies of the Cree, while Dakota and Lakota bands moved west. Nakoda and Dakota families later gathered at a government agency on the Missouri River, and after the 1876 Battle of the Little Bighorn some followers of the Lakota leaders Sitting Bull and Gall settled among them. Once the buffalo were gone, hunger set in. In an agreement ratified in 1888, the tribes gave up a huge shared territory across northern Montana and accepted the reservation's present boundaries, with the Missouri River as the southern edge. Allotment in the early 1900s opened much of the remaining land to homesteaders. Today the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes govern from Poplar, and Wolf Point is the largest town. Fort Peck Community College serves the reservation, and the tribes keep a bison herd that includes animals from Yellowstone.

summary: The Apsáalooke, known in English as the Crow, take their name from a word meaning children of the large-beaked bird. Their ancestors lived in earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River with the people who became the Hidatsa, and the two nations remain relatives. After the groups parted, the Apsáalooke moved west and made their home in the Yellowstone and Bighorn country of present-day Montana and Wyoming. The 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty recognized a vast Crow territory. The 1868 treaty cut it to a reservation south of the Yellowstone River, and later cessions reduced it again. Crow leaders, Plenty Coups among them, chose to ally with the United States and negotiate rather than fight, yet the government treated the Crow much as it treated other nations. When allotment was finished in the early 1920s, Crow negotiators had kept reservation land from being sold off as surplus, although a checkerboard of Indian and non-Indian ownership remains. The reservation covers about 2.2 million acres in south-central Montana, bordered by Wyoming on the south. Crow Agency is the seat of tribal government and home to Little Big Horn College. Many Apsáalooke speak Crow as their first language, and families gather each summer for Crow Fair.

summary: The Northern Cheyenne call themselves Tsis tsis'tas and are also known as the Morning Star People, in honor of the leader Morning Star, called Dull Knife in English. Cheyenne ancestors lived in present-day Minnesota and along the upper Missouri, growing corn, before taking up horses and buffalo hunting on the Plains. In time the nation divided, and the Southern Cheyenne are close relatives. After the 1876 Battle of the Little Bighorn, the Army attacked and destroyed much of a large Northern Cheyenne village. In 1877 they surrendered and were sent to Indian Territory, where many sickened and died. In September 1878, Morning Star and Little Wolf led a band north toward home. Soldiers captured part of the group in Nebraska, and many people were killed or died of hardship before the survivors reached Montana. In 1884 an executive order set aside a reservation on the Tongue River, later enlarged to its present boundaries. Today the reservation in southeastern Montana is almost entirely owned by the tribe and its members. Lame Deer is the seat of government and home to Chief Dull Knife College, where language programs help keep Cheyenne a living language.

summary: The Chippewa Cree Tribe, whose people call themselves Ne Hiyawak, joins two peoples. Chippewa bands once lived on both sides of today's Canadian border around the Great Lakes, and Cree territory reached from eastern Canada into Saskatchewan and Alberta. Over the 1700s and 1800s both moved west, and by the 1890s many had come together in Montana, looking for a permanent home. For years the followers of Chippewa leader Stone Child, whose name was mistranslated into English as Rocky Boy, and Cree leader Little Bear had no land of their own. They sheltered on the edges of Montana towns and on other reservations, and they suffered great hardship. With help from allies in Great Falls and Helena, the two chiefs kept pressing the federal government until 1916, when part of the old Fort Assiniboine military lands became Rocky Boy's Reservation. The reservation sits in the Bears Paw Mountains of north-central Montana. It was never allotted, and the whole of it is held in trust for the tribe. Later purchases enlarged it to about 122,000 acres. An elected Business Committee governs from Rocky Boy's Agency, and Stone Child College offers degrees close to home.

summary: The Blackfeet Nation calls its people Niitsitapi, the Real People. Members descend from three closely related peoples, the Siksika, the Kainai or Blood, and the Piikani or Piegan, who shared one language and a homeland reaching from the North Saskatchewan River in present-day Canada south toward Yellowstone. Horses and guns changed Blackfeet life in the 1700s and 1800s, and Blackfeet warriors earned the respect of neighboring nations. In 1855 the Blackfeet signed a treaty at the Judith River that set aside a large hunting territory shared with neighbors. Within two decades, executive orders and acts of Congress had cut it down. When the buffalo disappeared and government rations fell short, many Blackfeet died in the Starvation Winter of 1883 to 1884. An 1888 agreement drew the reservation's own boundaries. In the 1890s, under heavy pressure, the nation sold the mountain land that became much of Glacier National Park. How much land and money that agreement covered is still disputed, and the nation keeps certain rights there. Browning is the seat of the Blackfeet Tribal Business Council, whose nine members govern a reservation of about 1.5 million acres on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. Browning is also home to Blackfeet Community College and the Museum of the Plains Indian.

summary: The Little Shell Tribe of Chippewa Indians of Montana descends from Chippewa, Cree, and Métis families of the Red River, Pembina, and Turtle Mountain country along today's border with Canada. Many spoke Michif, a language that blends Chippewa, Cree, and French. The tribe takes its name from Chief Little Shell, whose band hunted buffalo and traded across the northern Plains and into Montana. In the late 1800s, as the government pressed to shrink the Turtle Mountain lands in North Dakota, Chief Little Shell refused to sign the new agreement, and many of his people were away hunting in Montana when government rolls were drawn up. Left off those rolls, they lost federal recognition and any claim to a reservation. For generations families lived without a land base, some on the edges of Montana towns and some among other tribes. Many worked as ranch hands or gathered buffalo bones to sell just to get by. Leaders such as Joseph Dussome kept the tribe organized and petitioning. After more than a century of effort, federal recognition came through an act of Congress in December 2019. The tribe is headquartered in Great Falls, where it has opened the Little Shell Tribal Cultural Center.

summary: The Northern Arapaho are one branch of the Arapaho people. Their Southern Arapaho relatives settled in what became Oklahoma, and the Aaniiih of Montana's Fort Belknap Reservation are also kin. Northern Arapaho elders still regard the plains and mountains of northern Colorado as their historic homeland. The Oregon Trail and the Colorado gold rush brought travelers, settlers, and conflict into Arapaho country. After Colorado troops attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village in the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre, war spread, and the northern and southern bands grew further apart. In 1868 the Northern Arapaho signed a treaty at Fort Laramie that promised them a reservation but named no place for it. For ten years they kept seeking a homeland of their own. In 1878 the government settled them, under Army escort, on the Eastern Shoshone reservation in Wyoming's Wind River Valley, and the two nations, once enemies, have shared it ever since. Today the Northern Arapaho Tribe lives mainly on the eastern side of the Wind River Reservation, with tribal offices in Ethete and Arapahoe. Royalties from oil found on tribally held land have supported members for decades.

summary: The Eastern Shoshone are the Shoshone nation of central Wyoming. They are related to the Shoshone, Bannock, Paiute, and Ute peoples of the Great Basin and to the Comanche of the southern Plains. The tribe's own history ties its people to the Wind River, Absaroka, and Yellowstone country for thousands of years. By fur-trade times they were a horse people who hunted buffalo east of the Continental Divide and traded at the trappers' rendezvous and later at Fort Bridger. Under their leader Washakie, the Eastern Shoshone negotiated with the United States as emigrant trails, gold mining, and the railroad crowded their lands. The 1863 Fort Bridger Treaty described a Shoshone homeland of about 44 million acres. The 1868 Fort Bridger Treaty replaced it with a far smaller reservation in the Wind River Basin, the Warm Valley that Washakie chose. Later cessions and allotment cut it further. In 1878 the government placed the Northern Arapaho, long their rivals, on the same reservation, which was later renamed the Wind River Reservation. Today the Eastern Shoshone live mainly on the western side of the reservation. The tribal government is based at Fort Washakie, the former Army post renamed for the chief.

summary: The Umoⁿhoⁿ, or Omaha, are a Dhegiha Siouan people whose name refers to going upstream, against the current. It recalls a long migration in which related peoples, among them the Ponca, Osage, Kaw, and Quapaw, took separate paths. The Omaha settled west of the middle Missouri River in present-day Nebraska, where they built earth lodges, raised corn, and hunted buffalo on the western plains. Epidemics and the upheavals of the fur trade took a heavy toll in the early 1800s. In an 1854 treaty the Omaha gave up most of their remaining Nebraska land in exchange for a reservation in the northeastern part of the state, and they moved there soon after. A decade later part of that reservation became the new home of the Ho-Chunk, or Winnebago. An 1882 act of Congress divided reservation land into individual allotments, and much of it was later sold or lost for unpaid taxes. The tribe organized a constitutional government with an elected council under the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934. Its headquarters are in Macy, Nebraska, where Nebraska Indian Community College has a campus. Many members also live in Omaha, Lincoln, and Sioux City.

summary: The Santee Sioux Nation is a Dakota nation whose people call themselves Isanti. Its members descend largely from the Mdewakanton and Wahpekute bands, part of the Santee division of the Dakota, who lived in the woodlands and lake country of present-day Minnesota, farming and living in villages for much of the year. Through a series of treaties the Dakota gave up most of their Minnesota land. Promised payments and supplies often failed to arrive, and hunger and distrust grew until war broke out in Minnesota in 1862. Afterward the Army imprisoned many Dakota people, and a military commission tried the accused without lawyers. The federal government then carried out a mass execution at Mankato and shipped Santee families by boat to Crow Creek in Dakota Territory, where many died of disease and hunger. In 1866 a presidential order set aside land along the Missouri River in northeastern Nebraska for the Santee at Crow Creek, and the people moved there. Allotment later cut the reservation sharply. Today the reservation lies in Knox County, Nebraska, with the Missouri River on its northern edge. The Santee campus of Nebraska Indian Community College teaches Dakota language and culture.

summary: The Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska are Ho-Chunk people, and Hocak is their language. Their ancestral homelands lie in present-day Wisconsin and northern Illinois. Beginning in the early 1800s, treaty after treaty took most of the nation's land, and the government moved the people again and again, from northeast Iowa to Minnesota. After the 1862 war in Minnesota, the government removed the Ho-Chunk along with the Santee Dakota to Crow Creek, on the treeless plains of present-day South Dakota. Life there was desperate, and many Ho-Chunk made their way down the Missouri River, often under cover of darkness, to join relatives in Nebraska. In 1865 the government moved the Ho-Chunk at Crow Creek to land that had been part of the Omaha Reservation, and treaties established the Winnebago Reservation there. Allotment after 1887 cost the nation much of that reservation, and population and economic opportunity declined for decades. The tribe later organized a constitutional government under the Indian Reorganization Act and put part of a land-claims award toward buying land back. The tribal government is based in the village of Winnebago, Nebraska, which is also home to Little Priest Tribal College.

summary: The Ponca Tribe of Nebraska calls its people P’ą́’k’a. Ponca oral history traces a long migration west with other Dhegiha peoples, including the Umoⁿhoⁿ (Omaha), Osage, Kaw, and Quapaw. The Ponca and Omaha traveled together longest. The Ponca made their home where the Niobrara River meets the Missouri in present-day northeastern Nebraska, raising corn, fishing, and hunting buffalo in spring and fall. The Ponca never went to war with the United States, yet treaties steadily shrank their land, and the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty with the Sioux gave the Ponca reservation to another nation. In 1877 the government forced the Ponca south to Indian Territory, and many died on the march and in the year that followed, including Chief Standing Bear's son. Standing Bear set out to bury him in the homeland, was arrested, and challenged his detention in federal court. In 1879 a federal judge in Omaha ruled that a Native American is a person under U.S. law. Standing Bear and many followers returned to the Niobrara, while other Ponca stayed in Oklahoma, where the Ponca Tribe of Oklahoma lives today. Congress terminated the northern tribe's federal status in the 1960s and restored it in 1990. The tribe is headquartered in Niobrara.

summary: The Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska, also known as the Ioway or Báxoje, is the nation for which the state of Iowa and the Iowa River were named. Archaeologists link the ancestral Ioway to the Oneota culture, and tribal tradition and language studies hold that the Ioway, Otoe, Missouria, Winnebago, and Omaha were once one people. Warfare in what is now Iowa pushed Ioway villages south into northern Missouri. By the late 1830s the nation had ceded its lands in Iowa and Missouri and moved west of the Missouri River to the Great Nemaha Reservation, where Presbyterian missionaries built a mission school that also served their Sac and Fox neighbors. In 1854 a treaty reduced the reservation, and that same year the new line between Kansas and Nebraska territories was drawn right across it, which is why the nation carries both names. In the late 1870s some families who opposed allotment moved to Indian Territory and became the Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma. Today the reservation straddles the Kansas–Nebraska line, with tribal headquarters near White Cloud, Kansas. In 2021 Kansas returned the old mission building and its grounds near Highland to the nation, which is restoring it as a museum.

summary: The Sac and Fox Nation of Missouri in Kansas and Nebraska, called Ne ma ha ha ki in the nation's own list of Sac and Fox peoples, is one of three federally recognized Sac and Fox nations. Its relatives are the Meskwaki, or Sac and Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa, and the Sa ki wa ki, or Sac and Fox Nation of Oklahoma. The Sauk, the People of the Yellow Earth, and the Fox, the Red Earth People, began as separate Algonquian-speaking woodland peoples who lived in bark houses in small villages. They drew together into a close alliance in the 1700s, and their history carries them through present-day Michigan, Wisconsin, Illinois, Iowa, and Missouri. The Missouri band came to be recognized as a distinct group in northern Missouri. In 1837 it moved west across the Missouri River to the Great Nemaha country of northeastern Kansas and southeastern Nebraska, next to the Ioway. Presbyterian missionaries soon opened a mission school there that served both nations. New treaties in the following decades sharply reduced their land, and white settlement followed. Today the nation's land lies in the northeastern corner of Kansas. Its museum in Reserve, Kansas, holds artifacts, photographs, and records of the nation's history.
